Where it began

Mark Butcher was born in Croydon on 23 August 1972, into a cricketing family. His father, Alan Butcher, played for Surrey and England, and his brother Gary played county cricket for Glamorgan and Surrey. Mark was playing for his school's under-11 side at the age of seven, and Surrey picked him up at under-11 and under-19 level.

He went to school at Cumnor House in Purley, then Trinity School and Archbishop Tenison's in Croydon. He played every one of his county games for Surrey, from his first-class debut in 1992 until he retired in 2009.

The player

He was a left-handed batsman who mostly opened, and a useful change bowler who could send down medium pace or off spin. His Test debut came at Edgbaston in the first Ashes Test of 1997, and England won by nine wickets.

Between 1997 and 2004 he played 71 Tests, scoring 4,288 runs at 34.58 with 8 hundreds and 23 fifties. He also took 15 wickets and held 61 catches, and in 1999 he led England once, in a drawn Test against New Zealand.

What made him special

His best-loved day came at Headingley in 2001. England needed 315 to beat Australia, and Butcher carried them there with 173 not out, one of the great fourth-innings knocks. It came after a lean spell in which his father's coaching helped him find his touch again, which made it all the sweeter.

By 2003–04 he was the man England turned to in a crisis. In the Caribbean that winter he passed fifty in four of his seven innings and made 296 runs, more than any of his teammates, as England won the series well. He played 42 Tests in a row for England. If he had a weakness, it was mornings: resuming overnight, he tended not to stay long. Plenty of batsmen would recognise the feeling.

Away from the middle

He is a gifted musician who sings and plays guitar. In 2001 he performed a Stranglers song live on BBC radio with the band's former frontman Hugh Cornwell, and his first album, Songs from the Sun House, came out in 2010. In 2007 he partnered Sarah Brightman on the BBC singing show Just the Two of Us, and they finished third.

After his playing days he became a commentator for Sky Sports and a summariser on Test Match Special, and he made a Sky documentary looking at why fewer Black cricketers were coming through in England. The MCC made him an honorary life member in January 2010.

And finally

He played 71 Tests without ever being picked for a one-day international, and by 2004 nobody else from the one-day era had played even half as many Tests without one. Of all the records a batsman might hold, being too good at the long game to be spared for the short one is not a bad one to have.
